source_text:
Quid mali, inquis, fieret, si et ista fierent summe bona? et tamen si quis ex nobis quaereret accepto et credito deo patre summo bono, si esset aliud summe bonum, unde esse nobis pie uideretur, nullo modo recte responderemus nisi de deo patre, qui summe bonus est. quod ergo de illo est, meminerimus natum de illo esse, non ab eo factum de nihilo, et ideo et hoc summe, id est incorruptibiliter bonum esse, uidemusque iniuste flagitari, ut tam summe bona sint, quae fecit de nihilo, quam summe bonus est, quem de se genuit: quem nisi unum genuisset, non id, quod ipse est, genuisset, quia ipse unus est. quapropter unico quidem filio, per quem facta sunt a patre omnia bona de nihilo, inperite atque inpie fratres quaeruntur, nisi ex eo, quod in homine adparere dignatus est. nam ideo et unigenitus in scripturis et primogenitus dicitur: unigenitus a patre, primogenitus ex mortuis. et uidimus, inquit, gloriam eius tamquam unigeniti a patre, pleni gratia et ueritate, et Paulus dicit: ut sit ipse primogenitus in multis fratribus.
Quodsi dixerimus "non iam essent ista bona, quae de nihilo facta sunt, sed tantummodo dei natura esset", inuidebimus tantis bonis et uox inpia est, iniuriam putare non hoc esse, quod deus est, et ideo nolle esse aliquod bonum, quoniam ei praeponitur deus. quaeso, patere, natura animae rationalis, aliquanto minus te esse quam deus est, et tanto minus, ut post ipsum te melius aliquid non sit, patere, inquam, et mitesce illi, ne te adhuc repellat in infima, ubi per angustias poenales etiam atque etiam bonum, quod es, uilescat tibi. superba es in deum, si indignaris, quod te antecedit, et nimis contumeliose de illo sentis, si non ineffabiliter gratularis tam magnum bonum esse te, ut solus sit ille praestantior. quo constituto atque firmato illud ne dixeris: me solam naturam deus facere debuit; nollem, ut post me aliquid boni fieret. non enim quod bonum est post deum, iam debuit esse nouissimum. et hinc maxime adparet, quantam tibi tribuerit dignitatem, quod deus, qui solus tibi naturaliter dominatur, fecit alia bona, quibus tu quoque dominareris. nec mireris, quod nunc tibi non omni modo seruiunt et te aliquando etiam cruciant, quia dominus tuus maiorem habet potestatem in ea, quae tibi seruiunt, quam tu ipsa, tamquam in seruos seruorum suorum. quid ergo mirum, si tibi peccanti, id est non obtemperanti domino tuo poenalia, quibus dominabaris, effecta sunt? quid enim tam iustum et quid iustius deo? hoc namque humana natura in Adam meruit, de quo nunc non est disputandi locus; sed tamen dominator iustus et iustis praemiis et iustis subpliciis adprobatur beatitate recte uiuentium poenaque peccantium. nec tamen sine misericordia derelicta es, quae certis rerum temporumque mensuris uocaris, ut redeas. ita recto moderamine altissimi conditoris usque ad bona terrena peruentum est, quae corrumpuntur et reformantur, ut haberes subplicio mixta solatia, ut et laudares deum delectata ordine bonorum, et refugeres in eum exercitata experimentis malorum. ita in quantum tibi terrena seruiunt, docent te esse dominam suam; in quantum autem molesta sunt, docent, ut seruias domino tuo.
thought_title: Why God made other goods below himself
orientation: Augustine is answering an imagined Manichaean objection that God should have made only himself, by explaining the order of goods and the rational soul's place below God.
pass_a_gloss: What evil, you say, would happen, if even these things were made supremely good? And yet if anyone from us were asked, after accepting and believing in God the Father as the supreme good, whether there is another supreme good, from where it would seem to us piously to be, in no way would we rightly answer except from God the Father, who is supremely good. Therefore what is from him, let us remember that it was born from him, not made by him from nothing, and therefore this too is supremely, that is incorruptibly, good, and we see that it is unjustly demanded that the things which he made from nothing be as supremely good as he whom he begot from himself is supremely good: whom if he had not begotten as one, he would not have begotten that which he himself is, because he himself is one. Wherefore for the only Son, through whom all good things were made from nothing by the Father, brothers are unskillfully and impiously sought, except from that which he deigned to appear as in man. For therefore he is called both only-begotten in the scriptures and first-born: only-begotten from the Father, first-born from the dead. And we have seen, he says, his glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth, and Paul says: that he himself might be first-born among many brothers. But if we shall have said 'these things which were made from nothing would no longer be good, but only the nature of God would exist', we shall envy such great goods, and it is an impious voice to think it an injury not to be that which God is, and therefore to be unwilling that there be any good, since God is preferred to it. I ask, allow, nature of the rational soul, that you be somewhat less than God is, and so much less that after him nothing better than you exists; allow, I say, and become gentle toward him, lest he still drive you back into the lowest places, where through penal straits again and again the good that you are may become worthless to you. You are proud against God, if you are indignant that he goes before you, and you think too insultingly about him, if you do not ineffably rejoice that you are so great a good that he alone is more excellent. When this has been established and made firm, do not say that: God ought to have made me alone as a nature; I would not wish that any good be made after me. For that which is good after God ought not already to have been the last. And from this it appears most of all how great a dignity he granted to you, that God, who alone naturally rules over you, made other goods over which you too might rule. And do not wonder that now they do not serve you in every way and sometimes even torment you, because your lord has greater power over those things which serve you than you yourself, as over servants of his servants. What wonder then, if for you sinning, that is not obeying your lord, the things over which you ruled were made penal? For what is so just and what more just than God? For this human nature merited in Adam, about which there is now no place to dispute; but nevertheless a just ruler is approved both by just rewards and by just punishments, by the blessedness of those living rightly and by the punishment of those sinning. Nor yet have you been abandoned without mercy, you who are called by fixed measures of things and times, so that you may return. Thus by the right governance of the most high founder one arrives even at earthly goods, which are corrupted and reformed, so that you might have consolations mixed with punishment, so that you might both praise God delighted by the order of goods, and flee back into him exercised by the experiences of evils. Thus insofar as earthly things serve you, they teach that you are their mistress; but insofar as they are troublesome, they teach that you should serve your lord.

choices.why: Renders the superlative adverb with adjective, matching the contrast with God as summe bonus.
Fixed glossary term for creation from nothing; kept literal.
Adverb preserved to show the manner of the Son's goodness, distinct from created goods.
Passive kept to preserve the impersonal demand Augustine criticizes; 'brothers' is literal for the Son's siblings.
Direct address to the soul as a nature; keeps the vocative force of the Latin.
Feminine form matches the soul addressed as feminine and the contrast with dominus.

pass_b_english: What harm would it do, you ask, if the things God made from nothing were also supremely good? And yet if one of us were asked, after accepting and believing in God the Father as the supreme good, whether there could be another supreme good and where it might piously be thought to come from, we could give no right answer except that it comes from God the Father, who is supremely good. So we must remember that what is from him was born from him, not made by him from nothing, and therefore it too is supremely good—that is, incorruptibly good. And we see that it is unjust to demand that the things he made from nothing should be as supremely good as the one he begot from himself, who is supremely good. If he had not begotten one alone, he would not have begotten what he himself is, because he himself is one. Therefore it is unskillful and impious to look for brothers for the only-begotten Son, through whom the Father made all good things from nothing, unless they are sought because he deigned to appear in human nature. For this reason he is called both only-begotten and first-born in the Scriptures: only-begotten from the Father, first-born from the dead. And, he says, we have seen his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). And Paul says: so that he might be the first-born among many brothers (Romans 8:29).

But if we were to say, "These good things that were made from nothing would no longer exist, but only God's nature would exist," we would be envying such great goods. It is an impious voice to think it an injury that a thing is not what God is, and therefore to wish that no good should exist because God is set above it. I ask you, nature of the rational soul, bear with being somewhat less than God is—and so much less that after him nothing is better than you. Bear with it, I say, and become gentle toward him, lest he drive you still further down into the depths, where through the narrow straits of punishment the good that you are may become utterly worthless to you. You are proud against God if you are indignant that he goes before you, and you think of him too insultingly if you do not rejoice beyond words that you are so great a good that he alone is more excellent than you.

Once this is settled and made firm, do not say: "God should have made my nature alone; I would not want any good to be made after me." For what is good after God need not already be the last. And here it becomes most evident how much dignity he gave you: God, who alone naturally rules over you, made other good things over which you too would rule. Do not be surprised that they do not now serve you in every way and sometimes even torment you, because your Lord has greater power over the things that serve you than you yourself do, as over the servants of his own servants. What wonder, then, if when you sinned—that is, when you did not obey your Lord—the things you ruled over became instruments of punishment for you? What is so just, and what is more just than God? For human nature deserved this in Adam, though this is not the place to discuss it. But still the just ruler is shown by just rewards and just punishments: by the blessedness of those who live rightly and the punishment of those who sin.

Yet you have not been abandoned without mercy, for you are called back to return by fixed measures of things and times. So by the right governance of the most high Creator one has come down even to earthly goods, which are corrupted and reformed, so that you might have comforts mixed with punishment, so that you might praise God when delighted by the order of good things, and flee back to him when trained by the experience of evils. In this way, insofar as earthly things serve you, they teach you that you are their mistress; but insofar as they trouble you, they teach you to serve your Lord.

problems.quote: And we have seen his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
problems.source_quote: et uidimus, inquit, gloriam eius tamquam unigeniti a patre, pleni gratia et ueritate
problems.why: 'inquit' marks this as Mani's quoted words, not narration; English omits attribution.
problems.fix: And, he says, we have seen his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
problems.ruling: 'inquit' = 'he says,' attributing quote to prior speaker (Mani), not narrator; omission misleads on source.

edits.old: And we have seen his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
edits.new: And, he says, we have seen his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14).

fixed: Added 'he says' to mark the quotation from John 1:14 as Mani's quoted words, matching 'inquit' in the source.

problems.quote: These good things that were made from nothing should not exist, but only God's nature should exist
problems.source_quote: non iam essent ista bona, quae de nihilo facta sunt, sed tantummodo dei natura esset
problems.why: Latin is past/subjunctive 'would no longer exist' not 'should not exist'; 'tantummodo…esset' = 'would be only God's nature'. English shifts to deontic 'should'.
problems.fix: These good things that were made from nothing would no longer exist, but only God's nature would exist
problems.ruling: Latin 'non iam essent' is counterfactual past 'would no longer be', not deontic 'should not exist'; 'tantummodo dei natura esset' = 'would be only God's nature'.

problems.quote: become worthless to you again and again
problems.source_quote: etiam atque etiam bonum, quod es, uilescat tibi
problems.why: etiam atque etiam intensifies the degradation, not repetition; 'again and again' misreads the phrase.
problems.fix: the good that you are may become utterly worthless to you
problems.ruling: etiam atque etiam intensifies 'become worthless,' not 'again and again'; misleads reader into repeated action.

problems.quote: For what is good after God did not have to be the last
problems.source_quote: non enim quod bonum est post deum, iam debuit esse nouissimum
problems.why: The English inverts the logic: Augustine says what is good after God need not be the last/final thing.
problems.fix: For what is good after God need not already be the last
problems.ruling: non enim = 'for [it is] not [the case]'; English 'did not have to be' inverts: Augustine says good after God IS not last.

edits.old: These good things that were made from nothing should not exist, but only God's nature should exist
edits.new: These good things that were made from nothing would no longer exist, but only God's nature would exist

edits.old: become worthless to you again and again
For what is good after God did not have to be the last
edits.new: For what is good after God need not already be the last

fixed: Changed 'should not exist' to 'would no longer exist' and 'should exist' to 'would exist' to match the Latin subjunctive 'non iam essent...esset'.
Changed 'again and again' to 'utterly' to match 'etiam atque etiam' as an intensifier, not repetition.
Changed 'did not have to be the last' to 'need not already be the last' to match 'iam debuit esse nouissimum'.

problems.quote: you have come down even to earthly goods
problems.source_quote: usque ad bona terrena peruentum est
problems.why: The Latin is impersonal/passive: 'it has come to earthly goods' or 'one has reached earthly goods'—the English 'you have come down' personifies and changes the construction. The subject is the soul's journey, but 'peruentum est' is not directly 'you have come down.'
problems.fix: one has come down even to earthly goods
problems.ruling: 'peruentum est' is impersonal passive 'it has been reached'; 'you have come down' wrongly changes voice and adds 'down' not in source.

edits.old: you have come down even to earthly goods
edits.new: one has come down even to earthly goods

fixed: Changed 'you have come down even to earthly goods' to 'one has come down even to earthly goods' because the source 'usque ad bona terrena peruentum est' is impersonal/passive, not second-person.

dismissed.quote: And, he says, we have seen his glory
dismissed.why: The 'inquit' introduces Scripture (John 1:14), not Mani. The English 'he says' wrongly suggests the Manichaean interlocutor speaks.
dismissed.note: 'He says' renders the Latin 'inquit' faithfully, and the John 1:14 citation makes clear who is speaking.
